analysis.one_liner: Taxes private fund managers' profit share as ordinary income instead of the lower capital-gains rate.
analysis.headline: Introduced February 6, 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee; no markup, vote, or floor action since, with 15 Democratic and Independent senators backing it and none opposing on the record.
analysis.plain_summary: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers are paid largely with a share of their funds' profits, called carried interest. Today that income is taxed at the lower capital-gains rate instead of the rates working people pay on wages. The bill would reclassify carried interest as ordinary income, extend the same treatment to profits from selling a fund manager's stake, and subject it to self-employment taxes that fund ordinary payroll-funded programs. It preserves capital-gains treatment for money managers genuinely invest out of their own pockets.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who pays taxes into the federal budget, since the change would collect more revenue from a small group of very high earners; the burden falls on investment managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships earning carried interest.

how_it_helps.text: The bill recharacterizes net capital gain on an investment-services partnership interest as ordinary income, so carried interest would be taxed at ordinary rates rather than capital-gains rates, subject to exceptions [S2][S3].
It imposes self-employment taxes on carried interest income, the same payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare and apply to wage income [S2][S3].

It closes related paths: gain from selling a carried-interest stake, distributions of property against carried interest, and similar arrangements at investment entities and special purpose acquisition companies would be treated as ordinary income [S2][S3].

It keeps a 20% capital-gains-style exception only for 'qualified capital interests' — money the manager actually contributed at risk, allocated like outside investors' money — so the change targets compensation for services, not genuine investment returns [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund partners earning carried interest, who would pay ordinary income rates (up to 37% plus payroll taxes) instead of the 20% capital-gains rate; their firms and investors could face higher management costs or restructuring.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private fund managers with carried interest

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves capital-gains treatment for managers' own invested capital ('qualified capital interests') and carves out domestic C corporations, certain REIT-owned real estate partnerships, publicly traded partnership exchanges for 10 years, and family partnerships, so some of the industry's arrangements would keep their tax advantage [S3].

Opponents argue carried interest rewards managers' own risk-taking and that higher taxes would push fund activity or fund managers overseas; supporters' own design acknowledges some returns are genuine capital, not compensation [S3].

The proposal adds significant complexity — new definitions, anti-abuse regulations, and a 40% penalty on underpayments — and the revenue at stake comes from a narrow group of taxpayers relative to the total federal deficit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward: taxing compensation for managing other people's money like compensation from any other job. The exceptions are necessary to spare genuine at-risk investment but leave openings for tax planning, and enforcement relies on regulations the Treasury would have to write. The revenue gain is real but modest in fiscal terms; the main effect is fairness — aligning one group of high earners' tax rate with everyone else's.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2025, and it has sat there without a hearing, markup, vote, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2025 in the Senate on February 6, 2025 [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill, all Democrats or Independents, and none of the 55 Senate Republicans signed on [S4].
The Finance Committee, to which the bill was referred, has not reported it out, and it has never received a floor vote in the Senate [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers are better off, since carried interest continues to be taxed at the 20% capital-gains rate while the bill sits unconsidered; the Senate majority is better off in that it controls the agenda and has spent none of it here.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private fund managers keep the tax break

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the sponsor.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader John Thune

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters are Democrats or Independents and none of the 55 Senate Republicans signed on; there has been no vote to show a fuller split.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Carried interest is the core of their compensation, and the bill would tax it at ordinary rates up to 37% plus self-employment tax instead of 20%. Their continued benefit from the lower rate comes at the cost of revenue every other taxpayer makes up.

Real estate held for rental or investment is a covered asset, so real estate fund carried interest is taxed as ordinary income too, though REIT-owned partnerships meeting the bill's tests keep their treatment. Fund managers' gains here rest on a rate ordinary earners do not get.

industries.industry: Wealth management and tax advisory services
industries.note: A business built on planning around carried interest would persist in advising on the bill's exceptions, family partnership rules, and anti-abuse guidance; the industry's gain lies in complexity rather than in any benefit to the public.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is in session, but the bill faces long odds: it sits in the Finance Committee under a chair from the party with zero cosponsors, no hearing or markup has been scheduled, and similar carried-interest bills have repeatedly died without a floor vote in prior congresses. The realistic path is that it dies at the end of this Congress without a vote.
